title: Pylon Compute x Redwood - partner kickstart and integration scope
summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and Pylon Compute to explore integration points across GPU hardware packaging, joint go-to-market, and technical validation plan. Key themes: private deployment support, SKU/profile compatibility, billing/reseller models, benchmarks on H100/A100 equivalents, and marketplace/channel onboarding.
topics: commercial models: reseller vs co-sell vs marketplace
next_steps: Maya (Redwood SE) to run micro-benchmarks on Pylon H-series firmware on A100-equivalent profile by 2025-10-18
Tom to share Pylon hardware spec sheet, driver/firmware matrix, and NMS API docs (link) by 2025-10-14
Alex to send draft partnership MOU and proposed commercial models (reseller + referral) by 2025-10-20
Jonah to add Pylon as an option in Redwood partner marketplace backlog and schedule an internal roadmap sync by 2025-10-23
Joint follow-up call scheduled 2025-10-22 at 10:00 PT for bench review and MOU discussion
action_items: Maya: run latency/throughput bench (chat & embedding workloads) against Pylon H100-like node (due 2025-10-18)
Tom: provide driver/firmware compatibility matrix and contact for NOC integration (due 2025-10-14)
Alex: circulate draft MOU and proposed revenue split scenarios (due 2025-10-20)
Dean: share example customer deployment topology and typical concurrency targets (due 2025-10-16)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE - Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Tom (Pylon): Tom here from Pylon - thanks, excited to chat.
[00:08] Priya (Pylon): Priya, cloud eng.
[00:10] Maya (SE - Redwood): Maya here from the Redwood infra team.
[00:12] Jonah (PM - Redwood): Jonah, product.
[00:14] Sara (Pylon): Sara from bizdev.
[00:16] Mike (Pylon): Mike, hardware arch.
[00:18] Alex: Awesome. Rough agenda — intro, technical surface, go-to-market / commercial, then next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Tom: Yep. For context, Pylon builds rack-scale GPU appliances — we have H-series (NVIDIA H100 compatible) and T-series (A100-ish) forks. We're looking at tighter integrations with inference platforms to get into enterprise sales channels.
[00:38] Maya: Nice. Quick clarifying question — when you say "H-series forks" are you shipping OEM systems with NVIDIA driver stack, or a forked runtime?
[00:46] Mike: We run a validated driver stack but with our own firmware layer for power/thermal. The NV driver is upstream, but we have custom firmware and a thin orchestration shim for scheduling.
[00:56] Priya: We're also targeting managed cloud partners that want a dedicated GPU SKU but with predictable SLAs.
[01:02] Alex: Good. From Redwood's side, we offer three deployment modes — hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For partners like you, customers often want co-located dedicated pools or an OEM-style private control plane.
[01:16] Sara: Can you elaborate on the private control plane? Security is a big ask for our enterprise buyers.
[01:21] Jonah: Sure — our Private product gives a customer-managed control plane deployed in their VPC or on-prem. We can integrate with KMS/HSM, SSO (SAML), audit logs, and keep model weights out of our hosted tenancy. We've done multi-tenant setups where the control plane runs in customer infra and connects to the Redwood runtime.
[01:36] Tom: So, would that require Pylon to pre-install any agents on the appliance? How do we handle the orchestration shim you mentioned?
[01:42] Maya: Typically we need a lightweight connector — a container or systemd unit that registers the node with Redwood and reports health/metrics. We can adapt to your NMS APIs. Important thing: low-latency path for KV cache and batching.
[01:53] Mike: Our NMS exposes a REST API and gRPC endpoints — we can accommodate that. There's also a small on-box REST proxy.
[01:59] Maya: Perfect. For performance, we want to test with real workloads — convo/chat with 2k seq and embeddings. We'll need a test image and kernel/driver versions.
[02:08] Priya: We'll share images. One thing — our firmware has a slight difference in clock governor affecting small-batch latency; want to make sure you're aware.
[02:16] Maya: That's helpful to know — could explain tail-latency variance. We'll include percentile analysis in the bench report.
[02:22] Tom: Commercially, we have three GTM models in mind: reseller where Pylon sells hardware + Redwood add-on; co-sell where both teams pitch; and marketplace listing where customers can subscribe to Redwood + Pylon nodes. Any opinion?
[02:34] Alex: All are viable. From Redwood's perspective, reseller is simpler to pilot — Pylon handles hardware, Redwood invoices for software usage or a bundle. Marketplace is attractive but needs integration work and legal. Co-sell tends to scale best for enterprise deals but requires joint plays and sales engineering enablement.
[02:49] Sara: What about revenue split expectations?
[02:51] Alex: Typically we run referral fees for early pilots (5-15%), then work toward an MPL (Marketplace) listing commission or reseller margin. We'll put numbers in the MOU.
[02:59] Mike: On the integration side, what's required for hardware certification?
[03:02] Maya: At minimum: driver/firmware matrix, kernel version, CUDA/CuDNN versions, and a test harness. We do a smoke test, perf bench, and long duration soak (24h). For dedicated nodes, we also validate multi-tenant isolation and KV cache behavior.
[03:17] Priya: Our ops team can provide images and a small fleet for testing — maybe 3 nodes with mixed H/T series.
[03:23] Maya: That's perfect. We'll run chat generation at 1-5 rps and embeddings throughput tests. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latencies and tokens/sec.
[03:32] Jonah: On the product side, one compatibility ask — can your management plane expose telemetry for token-level cost analysis? We like to show cost per token and route policies.
[03:40] Mike: We can expose per-job metrics and GPU utilization. Token-level might require hooking into the inference runtime counters, which we'd need to hook to your runtime agent.
[03:47] Maya: That's doable — our agent emits per-request timing and token counts. We can map them to GPU utilization traces.
[03:53] Tom: Security checklist — SOC 2 is table stakes for our customers. Do you have SOC or ISO reports?
[03:58] Alex: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 compliant. We can share the security pack and the audit scope after an NDA.
[04:06] Sara: Cool. For pilots, customers often ask about data residency. Can Redwood's private deployment run fully air-gapped?
[04:12] Jonah: We support an on-prem private control plane option that's air-gapped, yes. There are some feature tradeoffs (limited remote telemetry), but we can do it.
[04:21] Priya: One sticky point we've seen is firmware updates and responsibility — who patches what?
[04:26] Alex: Usually hardware vendors handle firmware and OS patching; Redwood manages the runtime/agent and model-serving software. We can agree on an RACI in the MOU.
[04:33] Tom: Makes sense. Are there known incompatibilities — quantization paths, tensor cores, or HBM differences — we should be aware of?
[04:41] Maya: We test quantized execution paths and per-model kernel selection. If your H-series clocks behave differently, we might adjust kernel heuristics. We'll flag any perf delta against our canonical profiles.
[04:51] Dean: From product — customer types: enterprise SaaS, fintech, and gov. Many will want RBAC + audit and long retention. How does that map?
[04:59] Jonah: We can tune log retention and integrate with SIEMs. RBAC/SAML and per-route policies already exist. For long-term retention we offer enterprise add-ons.
[05:08] Tom: For the benchmark, do you need us to ship an image or provide a networked test cluster?
[05:13] Maya: Either works. Networked cluster is easiest to simulate production. If shipping is easier, we can also run tests on your hardware in our lab.
[05:21] Priya: We'll have a small lab cluster and can also let you run remote. We'll follow up with what is best.
[05:26] Alex: Cool. Any immediate red flags?
[05:29] Mike: Only concern is we need clear expectations on support SLAs — enterprise buyers expect 24/7 for certain customers.
[05:35] Alex: Redwood offers tiered SLAs for Dedicated and Private customers — we can align on response times in the MOU.
[05:40] Sara: Sales enablement — what collateral do you need from us?
[05:44] Clara (Redwood Solutions): One-pager on joint solution, top customer stories, and a tech-runbook are helpful.
[05:49] Sara: We'll prepare a partner one-pager and a joint slide deck.
[05:52] Tom: Let's talk timelines — we want a pilot in Q4. Realistic?
[05:56] Alex: Yes — if we start validation this week and the benches run in two weeks, a Q4 pilot is feasible. We'll need the MOU signed for reseller pilots.
[06:05] Maya: I'll lead the bench work — need access to node images and keys.
[06:09] Priya: We'll provide images and a test NMS endpoint.
[06:12] Jonah: I'll draft the MOU template and loop legal.
[06:15] Alex: Great. Quick recap and owners?
[06:18] Maya: Bench and perf — Maya (Redwood) with Pylon lab nodes (due 2025-10-18).
[06:23] Tom: Provide firmware/driver matrix and NMS API — Tom/Priya (due 2025-10-14).
[06:28] Alex: MOU and commercial models — Alex (due 2025-10-20).
[06:31] Dean: We'll send example customer topology — Dean (due 2025-10-16).
[06:34] Sara: Partner one-pager and slides — Sara (due 2025-10-17).
[06:37] Alex: Any final Qs?
[06:39] Mike: Nothing else from hardware.
[06:41] Priya: All good.
[06:43] Alex: Cool — we'll follow up with calendar invite for 2025-10-22. Thanks everyone.
[06:48] Tom: Thanks, talk soon.
[06:50] [END] 

NOTES: Transcription has occasional minor word swaps ("H-series forks" = Pylon's H100 variant). References to docs: Pylon spec sheet (to be shared), Redwood security pack (link after NDA), Redwood bench harness (https://redwood.ai/bench/harness).
